## 任务：撰写论文 Related Work Section

你是 ML 论文写作 Worker。任务：为 EACL 2027 ARR 投稿撰写 Related Work 章节。

## 输出
将完整 LaTeX 内容写入：
`/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0519_2/projects/xling_calib_direction/docs/paper/related_work.tex`

格式：纯 section 内容（`\section{Related Work}` 开头），不含 preamble。ACL 2023 双栏格式。

## 写作前必读
1. `Read /home/ubuntu/agent-ml-research/skills/global/paper-writing-norms.skill.md` — 写作规范
2. `Read /home/ubuntu/agent-ml-research/skills/global/latex-paper.skill.md` — LaTeX 规范

## 核心要求
- **1.5-2 页双栏**（约 1000 words + 对比表格）
- 审稿 R2-W1 指出原 Related Work 仅 15 行，必须大幅扩展
- 分 **5 个子方向**，每个方向 2-3 段
- 每个方向末尾一句话明确区分我们的工作
- 包含一个 **method×feature 对比表格**（Table 1）

## 5 个子方向结构

### 2.1 LLM Calibration and Internal Representations
**覆盖论文**：
- Guo et al. 2017 (temperature scaling, calibration fundamentals) — `\cite{guo2017calibration}`
- Kadavath et al. 2022 (verbalized confidence, "Know What You Know") — `\cite{kadavath2022language}` % [TO_ADD_BIB]
- Miao & Ungar 2026 (correctness-confidence orthogonality, cosine < 0.04) — `\cite{miao2026closing}`
- CORAL / Miao et al. 2026 (cross-task correctness probes, ~50% ECE improvement) — `\cite{miao2026coral}`
- CCPS / Khanmohammadi 2025 (perturbed representation stability) — `\cite{khanmohammadi2025ccps}`
- Confidence Manifold 2026 (3-8 dim structure, 25 examples → 89%) — `\cite{confidence_manifold2026}`
- Joshi 2025 (calibration across layers) — `\cite{joshi2025calibration}`
- Ji 2025 (verbal uncertainty linear direction) — `\cite{ji2025calibrating}`

**叙事**：从 post-hoc calibration (Guo) → verbalized confidence (Kadavath) → internal representation probing (Miao, CORAL, CCPS, Confidence Manifold) → layer-wise evolution (Joshi)。
**区分**：All English-only, single architecture. We extend to multilingual multi-architecture setting.

### 2.2 Cross-Lingual Probing and Transfer
**覆盖论文**：
- Xiao et al. ACL 2025 (knowledge boundary probing, 8 languages) — `\cite{xiao2025knowledge}`
- Civelli 2026 (difficulty probe, shared geometry, IRT) — `\cite{civelli2026shared}`
- DALI / Ravisankar 2026 (activation patching, causal evidence, 24 languages) — `\cite{ravisankar2026dali}`
- Liu & Niehues 2025 (middle-layer alignment in fine-tuned LLMs) — `\cite{liu2025middle}`
- MUSE / Conneau et al. 2018 — `\cite{conneau2018muse}` % [TO_ADD_BIB]
- VecMap / Artetxe et al. 2018 — `\cite{artetxe2018vecmap}` % [TO_ADD_BIB]

**叙事**：Knowledge boundary probing (Xiao) shows partial cross-lingual transfer but probes answerability (input-level), not correctness (output-dependent). Civelli probes difficulty (question property), not model correctness. DALI provides causal evidence that English middle-layer representations can fix non-English errors. MUSE/VecMap established linear projection for cross-lingual alignment.
**区分**：We probe correctness (output-dependent accuracy), not answerability or difficulty. We provide depth analysis with Pareto frontier, 5 transfer methods including linear projection, and 20 languages.

### 2.3 Multilingual Calibration
**覆盖论文**：
- LACE / Zhou et al. 2025 (adaptive layer ensemble, 5x ECE gap, 100+ languages) — `\cite{zhou2025lace}`
- Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana 2005 (Platt scaling) — `\cite{niculescu2005predicting}` % [TO_ADD_BIB]

**叙事**：Zhou et al. confirmed a 5x ECE gap between English and non-English languages across 100+ languages. LACE addresses this via per-language layer ensemble but requires per-language validation data.
**区分**：Our approach requires zero target-language correctness labels. We analyze WHY transfer fails (architecture-dependent Pareto, geometric CKA analysis), not just HOW to compensate.

### 2.4 Domain Adaptation Theory
**覆盖论文**：
- Ben-David et al. 2010 (H-divergence framework) — `\cite{bendavid2010theory}`
- Zhao et al. 2019 (invariant representations, conditional shift failure) — `\cite{zhao2019invariant}`

**叙事**：Ben-David's H-divergence framework predicts that cross-lingual probe transfer degrades with domain divergence (language distance). Zhao et al. prove that marginal distribution matching fails when conditional distributions $P(Y|X)$ differ between domains. This directly explains our CaCLR finding: MMD matches marginal distributions of probe logits but cannot align conditional structure.
**区分**：We empirically test these theoretical predictions in the correctness probing setting and provide geometric CKA analysis revealing a Simpson's Paradox not predicted by prior theory.

### 2.5 Probing Methodology and Evaluation
**覆盖论文**：
- Hewitt & Liang 2019 (control tasks, selectivity) — `\cite{hewitt2019control}`
- Voita & Titov 2020 (MDL probes) — `\cite{voita2020mdl}`
- Belinkov 2022 (probing survey) — `\cite{belinkov2022probing}`
- CKA / Kornblith et al. 2019 — `\cite{kornblith2019cka}`
- Angelopoulos & Bates 2023 (conformal prediction) — `\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}`

**叙事**：Hewitt & Liang's control task framework guards against capacity artifacts. We apply this to cross-lingual probing and find ~28% low-resource results are artifacts. CKA (Kornblith) measures representational similarity; we apply partial correlation revealing Simpson's Paradox. Conformal prediction (Angelopoulos & Bates) offers complementary distribution-free coverage guarantees but requires per-language calibration data.
**区分**：First application of probing controls to cross-lingual transfer. CKA partial correlation analysis is novel geometric insight.

在 §2.2 或 §2.3 后插入，格式：

```latex
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Comparison with closely related work on calibration probing and cross-lingual transfer.}
\label{tab:related_work}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
& \textbf{Target} & \textbf{\# Langs} & \textbf{Calib.} & \textbf{Zero-CL} & \textbf{Depth} & \textbf{Transfer} \\
& \textbf{Signal} & & \textbf{Metrics} & \textbf{Labels} & \textbf{Analysis} & \textbf{Methods} \\
\midrule
Xiao et al. & KB & 8 & — & \cmark & \xmark & 1 \\
LACE & — & 100+ & \cmark & \xmark & partial & — \\
CORAL & Corr. & 1 & \cmark & — & \cmark & 1 \\
Miao \& Ungar & Corr. & 1 & \xmark & — & \xmark & — \\
Civelli et al. & Diff. & 7 & \xmark & \cmark & \cmark & 1 \\
\midrule
\textbf{Ours} & \textbf{Corr.} & \textbf{20} & \textbf{\cmark} & \textbf{\cmark} & \textbf{\cmark} & \textbf{5} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

表头说明：
- Target Signal: KB=knowledge boundary, Corr.=correctness, Diff.=difficulty
- Calib. Metrics: 是否报告 ECE/Brier (不只是 probing accuracy)
- Zero-CL Labels: 是否不需要 target-language correctness labels
- Depth Analysis: 是否有跨层分析
- Transfer Methods: 测试了几种 transfer method

用 `\cmark` / `\xmark` 表示有/无。如果 amssymb/pifont 不可用，用 \checkmark 和 $\times$。在 preamble 或文件顶部加 `% Requires: \usepackage{pifont} \newcommand{\cmark}{\ding{51}} \newcommand{\xmark}{\ding{55}}` 注释。

## 写作风格硬规则
1. **禁止论文堆砌**（"A proposed X. B proposed Y. C proposed Z."）—— 做归纳和比较
2. 禁止 em-dash (—)，用逗号或括号替代
3. 禁止 -ing 短语结尾
4. 禁止连续 Furthermore/Moreover/Additionally
5. 禁止 "leverage"/"utilize"/"delve into"
6. 段落 5-8 句，不过度分段
7. 每个子方向末尾必须有 1 句话区分我们的工作
8. Booktabs 表格规范（\toprule/\midrule/\bottomrule，无竖线，无 \hline）
9. 使用 "zero-correctness-label" 而非 "zero-label"

|-------|-------------|----------------|

4	\section{Related Work}
5	
6	\subsection{LLM Calibration and Internal Representations}
7	
8	Post-hoc calibration methods such as temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} and Platt scaling \cite{niculescu2005predicting} treat model confidence as a scalar output to be recalibrated after training. These approaches assume access to a held-out validation set from the target distribution and operate entirely on output logits without inspecting internal representations.
9	A complementary line of work examines whether models can self-assess correctness through verbalized confidence. \citet{kadavath2022language} demonstrate that larger language models produce well-calibrated probability estimates when asked to evaluate their own answers, establishing that calibration information exists within the model prior to output generation.
10	
11	Recent studies shift attention from output-level calibration to representation-level probing. \citet{miao2026closing} identify that correctness and verbalized confidence occupy nearly orthogonal subspaces in hidden states (cosine similarity below 0.04), suggesting that standard confidence elicitation fails to capture the full calibration signal. Building on this observation, CORAL \cite{miao2026coral} trains correctness probes that transfer across tasks within English, achieving approximately 50\% ECE improvement over verbalized confidence baselines. CCPS \cite{khanmohammadi2025ccps} takes a complementary approach by measuring representation stability under input perturbations as a proxy for correctness. The Confidence Manifold framework \cite{confidence_manifold2026} reveals that calibration-relevant information concentrates in a low-dimensional subspace (3 to 8 dimensions), with as few as 25 labeled examples sufficient for 89\% probing accuracy. \citet{ji2025calibrating} further demonstrate that verbal uncertainty in LLMs corresponds to a linear direction in representation space, while \citet{joshi2025calibration} analyze how calibration signals evolve across layers, finding non-monotonic patterns that motivate layer selection.
12	
13	All of these studies operate exclusively in English and on a single model architecture. Our work extends correctness probing to 20 languages across 4 architectures, revealing that the geometric properties identified in English (orthogonality, low-dimensional manifold) do not transfer uniformly across languages.
14	
15	\subsection{Cross-Lingual Probing and Transfer}
16	
17	Cross-lingual probing investigates whether linguistic or behavioral properties encoded in one language's representations generalize to others. \citet{xiao2025knowledge} probe knowledge boundaries across 8 languages and find partial cross-lingual transfer, but their target signal is answerability (an input-level property) rather than correctness (which depends on the model's actual output). \citet{civelli2026shared} probe item difficulty using IRT-derived labels and report shared geometric structure across 7 languages; however, difficulty is a property of the question itself, independent of any particular model's response. DALI \cite{ravisankar2026dali} provides causal evidence through activation patching that English middle-layer representations can repair errors in 24 non-English languages, confirming that transferable correctness information exists but not quantifying when and why transfer fails.
18	
19	The technical foundations for cross-lingual alignment predate LLM-era probing. MUSE \cite{conneau2018muse} established adversarial training for unsupervised bilingual word embedding alignment, while VecMap \cite{artetxe2018vecmap} demonstrated that self-learning with structural similarity initialization achieves robust cross-lingual mappings without parallel data. \citet{liu2025middle} show that middle layers of fine-tuned LLMs exhibit stronger cross-lingual alignment than early or late layers, consistent with the depth patterns we observe for correctness probes.
20	
21	Our work differs in three respects: we probe correctness (an output-dependent signal that requires generating and evaluating answers), we provide systematic depth analysis with Pareto frontier characterization across architectures, and we evaluate 5 transfer methods (including linear projection inspired by MUSE/VecMap) across 20 languages.
22	
23	\subsection{Multilingual Calibration}
24	
25	Calibration quality varies dramatically across languages. \citet{zhou2025lace} document a 5$\times$ ECE gap between English and low-resource languages across 100+ languages and propose LACE, an adaptive layer ensemble that selects different layer combinations per language. While effective, LACE requires per-language validation data with correctness labels, limiting applicability to languages where such annotations exist.
26	
27	\begin{table}[t]
28	\centering
29	\small
30	\caption{Comparison with closely related work on calibration probing and cross-lingual transfer. Target signals: KB = knowledge boundary, Corr.\ = correctness, Diff.\ = difficulty. Zero-CL = zero target-language correctness labels required.}
31	\label{tab:related_work}
32	\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
33	\toprule
34	& \textbf{Target} & \textbf{\# Langs} & \textbf{Calib.} & \textbf{Zero-CL} & \textbf{Depth} & \textbf{Transfer} \\
35	& \textbf{Signal} & & \textbf{Metrics} & \textbf{Labels} & \textbf{Analysis} & \textbf{Methods} \\
36	\midrule
37	Xiao et al. & KB & 8 & \xmark & \cmark & \xmark & 1 \\
38	LACE & -- & 100+ & \cmark & \xmark & partial & -- \\
39	CORAL & Corr. & 1 & \cmark & -- & \cmark & 1 \\
40	Miao \& Ungar & Corr. & 1 & \xmark & -- & \xmark & -- \\
41	Civelli et al. & Diff. & 7 & \xmark & \cmark & \cmark & 1 \\
42	\midrule
43	\textbf{Ours} & \textbf{Corr.} & \textbf{20} & \cmark & \cmark & \cmark & \textbf{5} \\
44	\bottomrule
45	\end{tabular}
46	\end{table}
47	
48	The fundamental challenge that LACE addresses (per-language calibration heterogeneity) motivates our investigation, but our approach differs in both goal and mechanism. We analyze \emph{why} cross-lingual transfer of correctness probes fails (architecture-dependent depth-transferability tradeoffs, geometric divergence measured by CKA) rather than engineering a per-language compensation. Our method requires zero target-language correctness labels, transferring probes trained on English data alone.
49	
50	\subsection{Domain Adaptation Theory}
51	
52	The theoretical framework of \citet{bendavid2010theory} bounds target-domain error by source error plus a divergence term ($\mathcal{H}$-divergence) between source and target distributions, plus a joint ideal error. Applied to cross-lingual probe transfer, this predicts degradation proportional to the representational distance between languages. \citet{zhao2019invariant} prove a stronger negative result: when conditional distributions $P(Y|X)$ differ between domains, matching marginal distributions of representations can \emph{increase} target error rather than reduce it.
53	
54	This theoretical insight directly explains our empirical finding on CaCLR (Cross-lingual Calibration via Conditional Label-aware Representation matching). CaCLR applies MMD-based distributional matching to align probe activations across languages, but consistently underperforms simple linear projection. The explanation follows from \citet{zhao2019invariant}: because conditional accuracy distributions $P(\text{correct}|\mathbf{h})$ differ between languages (due to varying model competence), marginal alignment destroys the conditional structure that probes rely on. Our CKA partial correlation analysis further reveals a Simpson's Paradox where aggregate cross-lingual similarity masks within-layer divergence, a phenomenon not predicted by existing domain adaptation theory.
55	
56	\subsection{Probing Methodology and Evaluation}
57	
58	The methodological foundations of representation probing inform our experimental design. \citet{hewitt2019control} introduce control tasks that establish selectivity baselines, guarding against probes that succeed merely due to high capacity rather than genuine information in representations. \citet{voita2020mdl} propose minimum description length probes as an information-theoretic alternative, measuring the amount of effort required to extract a property. \citet{belinkov2022probing} surveys the broader landscape of probing classifiers, identifying best practices and common pitfalls including the capacity-informativeness tradeoff.
59	
60	We apply the control task framework of \citet{hewitt2019control} to cross-lingual correctness probing and find that approximately 28\% of positive transfer results in low-resource languages are capacity artifacts (probes achieve similar accuracy on shuffled labels). This finding underscores the importance of probing controls in multilingual settings where target-language data scarcity can inflate apparent transfer success. For measuring representational similarity across languages and layers, we employ CKA \cite{kornblith2019cka} with partial correlation analysis, revealing geometric structure invisible to standard pairwise comparisons. Conformal prediction \cite{angelopoulos2023conformal} offers distribution-free coverage guarantees complementary to our probing approach but requires per-language calibration data, which our zero-correctness-label setting explicitly avoids.
61	
62	Our work contributes the first systematic application of probing controls to cross-lingual transfer evaluation and introduces CKA partial correlation as a diagnostic tool for understanding transfer failure modes.

DALI \cite{ravisankar2026dali} provides causal evidence through activation patching that English middle-layer representations can repair errors in 24 non-English languages, which confirms that transferable correctness information exists but does not quantify when or why probe-level transfer fails. This gap motivates three research questions: (1) Does the correctness direction persist across languages, or is it language-specific? (2) How does cross-lingual transfer depend on representation geometry, specifically layer depth and cross-lingual representational similarity? (3) Can distributional matching shift the transfer frontier without target-language correctness labels?

We present the first large-scale study of correctness probe transfer across architectures. The study covers 2+ model families, 20 languages in three resource tiers, and 5 transfer methods evaluated on GlobalMMLU. Our central finding is an architecture-dependent depth-transferability tradeoff (Figure~\ref{fig:pareto}): deeper layers yield better English probe quality but degrade cross-lingual transfer. The shape of this Pareto frontier varies across architectures: Qwen exhibits a strong monotonic tradeoff, while Llama displays language-specific patterns.

This tradeoff conceals a deeper geometric structure. The raw correlation between Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) \cite{kornblith2019cka} and transfer Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC) across all language-layer pairs is negative, because both quantities covary with depth. After controlling for depth via partial correlation, the sign reverses: within each layer, higher cross-lingual CKA predicts better probe transfer ($\rho = +0.41$, $p = 0.006$ in pilot analysis). This Simpson's Paradox exposes a confounding pattern that naive cross-layer pooling obscures: what appears as a negative CKA-transfer association in aggregate is in fact a positive within-layer relationship.

A methodological finding further qualifies these results. We apply the control task framework of \citet{hewitt2019control} to cross-lingual probing and find that approximately 28\% of positive transfer results in low-resource languages are capacity artifacts, where probes achieve similar accuracy on shuffled labels. This is the first application of probing controls to cross-lingual transfer evaluation and constitutes a field-level warning for the community. On the practical side, linear projection via Procrustes alignment achieves near-optimal transfer with approximately 50 parallel sentence pairs, though saturation rate depends on resource tier. We also design Calibration-aware Cross-Lingual Regularization (CaCLR), a distributional matching objective ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SB-ECE}} + \beta \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{consistency}}$), as a principled test of whether Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) alignment can improve zero-correctness-label transfer (results pending experimental validation).

Our experimental framework provides systematic coverage along four axes. We test 2+ architectures (Qwen3-235B-A22B and Llama 4 Scout 17B-16E as primary models) across 20 languages that span high, medium, and low resource tiers. We compare 5 transfer methods ordered by complexity: zero-shot application, mean-shift alignment, Procrustes rotation, few-shot probe retraining, and CaCLR (\S\ref{sec:transfer}). All transfer methods except few-shot retraining satisfy a zero-correctness-label constraint and need no target-language correctness annotations. We decompose probe targets into difficulty-shared and capability-specific components through IRT-based projection (\S\ref{sec:decomposition}), which explains why transfer succeeds at some layers and fails at others. CKA geometric analysis with depth-controlled partial correlation provides the diagnostic framework to explain failure modes (\S\ref{sec:geometric}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Architecture-dependent Pareto frontier and CKA geometric analysis.} We discover that cross-lingual correctness probe transfer exhibits a depth-transferability tradeoff whose shape varies across architectures. A Simpson's Paradox in the CKA-transfer relationship reveals that within-layer representational similarity predicts transfer success, a confounding pattern obscured by naive cross-layer pooling (\S\ref{sec:geometric}).

\item \textbf{Difficulty-capability decomposition.} We decompose cross-lingual transfer into a difficulty-shared component (transferable at all depths) and a capability-specific component (responsible for deep-layer degradation), which yields prescriptive predictions for alignment strategy selection (\S\ref{sec:decomposition}).

\item \textbf{CaCLR distributional matching test.} We design CaCLR ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SB-ECE}} + \beta \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{consistency}}$) as a principled baseline that tests whether MMD-based distributional matching can improve zero-correctness-label transfer. Results are pending experimental validation (\S\ref{sec:transfer}).

\item \textbf{Empirical contributions with practical implications.} (a) Control task analysis reveals that approximately 28\% of low-resource probing results are capacity artifacts, a field-level methodological warning (\S\ref{sec:controls}). (b) Linear projection with approximately 50 parallel pairs achieves near-optimal transfer with resource-tier-dependent saturation. (c) Procrustes alignment exhibits effect reversal: it helps when zero-shot AUROC $< 0.50$ but degrades performance when zero-shot AUROC $> 0.60$ (\S\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}
